Three and a Half
THREE and uh HAF
n.
A composite numeral appearing in Scripture as three distinct equivalent expressions: time, times, and half a time (Aramaic iddan w’idanin u-plag iddan, Dan 7:25; 12:7; Rev 12:14); forty-two months (Rev 11:2; 13:5); and one thousand two hundred and sixty days (Rev 11:3; 12:6). All three measure the same period: half of seven, the compressed age of the beast’s temporary authority.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Three and a half is Scripture’s number for the period of permitted tribulation — a time of suffering that is real, severe, and sovereignly bounded. It is half of seven: the covenant number of God’s complete and perfect purpose, fractured to its midpoint. The threefold expression of the same period — “time, times, and half a time,” “forty-two months,” and “one thousand two hundred and sixty days” — is not three different eras but one theological reality seen from three angles, all originating in Daniel and completed in Revelation. In Daniel 7:25 the little horn speaks against the Most High and wears out the saints for “a time, times, and half a time” before the court sits and his dominion is taken away. In Daniel 12:7 the angel swears by the Living God that these words shall be fulfilled when the power of the holy people is completely shattered — a point of utter human weakness from which only God can deliver. Revelation deploys all three expressions: the nations trample the holy city for forty-two months (Rev 11:2); the two witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days (Rev 11:3); the woman flees into the wilderness for time, times, and half a time (Rev 12:14); the beast exercises authority for forty-two months (Rev 13:5). The theological import is fixed: the period of the beast’s apparent triumph is not an eternal reign but a permitted and measured time, always already half over because God’s seven still stands. The saints endure for three and a half; they shall reign for ever and ever.

Webster 1828 Definition

Three and a half: the biblical measurement of the age of permitted tribulation, expressed as time-times-half-a-time, forty-two months, and 1,260 days — half of seven, the fractured covenant period bounded by God’s sovereign decree.

THREE AND A HALF, n. In Scripture, the number of the beast’s allotted season and the church’s wilderness sojourn: real suffering, real duration, but measured and bounded. The creature-empire is never given a full seven; it receives only half — which is to say, God’s sovereign decree has already placed a terminus on every earthly tyranny.

The three equivalent expressions (time-times-half-a-time, 42 months, 1,260 days) are not competing chronologies but a theological triplet, each angle clarifying the same reality: the period of tribulation is appointed, measured, and therefore endurable.

Key Scripture

Daniel 12:7 — "Then I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by Him who lives forever, that it shall be for a time, times, and half a time; and when the power of the holy people has been completely shattered, all these things shall be finished."

Revelation 11:9 — "And those from the peoples and tribes and tongues and nations look at their dead bodies for three and a half days. And they do not permit their dead bodies to be laid in a tomb."

Revelation 12:14 — "And the two wings of the great eagle were given to the woman — so that she could fly into the wilderness to her place, where she is nourished for a time, and times, and half a time, away from the presence of the serpent."

Daniel 9:27 — "Then he shall confirm a covenant with many for one week; but in the middle of the week he shall bring an end to sacrifice and offering."

Modern Corruption

Dispensationalist prophetic charts assign three and a half years to a literal future Great Tribulation within a seven-year parenthesis of history, divorcing the Danielic period from its first-century fulfillment and generating a complex architecture of “gaps” unknown to the apostolic authors.

expand to see more

In classic dispensationalist eschatology, the three-and-a-half expressions refer to the second half of a future seven-year tribulation period — specifically the forty-two months of the Antichrist’s visible reign following the abomination of desolation. This requires inserting a gap between the sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks of Daniel 9 sufficient to span all of church history, then literalizing the forty-two months as a precise future calendar. Reformed, amillennial, and preterist interpreters hold that the apostolic authors themselves understood the period as the age of the church under pagan Rome, or as already fulfilled in the events of AD 66–70.

Charismatic prophecy culture sometimes treats 1,260 as a secret numeric key unlocking end-times timelines, forgetting that John’s concern is not calendar arithmetic but the perseverance of the saints. The wilderness sojourn of three and a half is not a period to predict but a pattern to recognize and endure — the church nourished by God in the wilderness while the dragon rages, always already under God’s protective wing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Aramaic origin of the expression in Daniel roots it in the experience of exilic Israel under pagan empire; Revelation translates it into three equivalent Greek expressions, establishing its character as a theological constant for the age of the church.

expand to see more

Aramaic iddan w’idanin u-plag iddan — time, times, and half a time; the original expression in Daniel 7:25 and 12:7.

Greek tessarakonta [kai] duo mēnas — forty-two months; used in Rev 11:2 and 13:5.

Greek chilías diakosías hexkonta hēméras — one thousand two hundred sixty days; used in Rev 11:3 and 12:6.

Seven divided by two — the covenant number fractured to its midpoint, always implying the other half that God holds in reserve.

Historicist reading: the 1,260 days as prophetic years (day-year principle), spanning from Rome’s rise to the Reformation or the end of the age.

Usage

"The fact that three and a half appears as three equivalent expressions — not as three different periods — is itself the message: God’s sovereignty over the beast’s allotted time is so certain that He can name it three ways and the arithmetic always converges."

"The woman nourished in the wilderness for time, times, and half a time is the church: real suffering, real exile, real conflict with the serpent — but sustained by God and therefore undefeated."

"Three and a half is the number of “not yet seven” — the tribulation is always penultimate, always bounded, always awaiting the completion that only God’s full seven will bring."
